lessons.title: The Palestinians and Lebanon, 1974–87
lessons.description: How the PLO went from the UN podium to a Beirut siege and Tunisian exile in eight years.
lessons.content_html:
Rabat 1974 — A Diplomatic Coronation

In October 1974, twenty Arab heads of state met at Rabat and declared the Palestine Liberation Organisation, led by Yasser Arafat, the ‘sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people’. The Rabat resolution mattered because it stripped King Hussein of Jordan of his long-standing claim to speak for the Palestinians of the West Bank, lost to Israel in 1967. From now on, any Israeli withdrawal from the West Bank would have to be negotiated with the PLO. A month later, on 13 November 1974, Arafat addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York, his pistol holster prominent on his belt. ‘Today I have come bearing an olive branch and a freedom-fighter’s gun’, he said. ‘Do not let the olive branch fall from my hand.’ The assembly granted the PLO permanent observer status. For one year, the Palestinian cause looked diplomatically unstoppable.

Key Fact

At Rabat in October 1974 the Arab League declared the PLO the ‘sole legitimate representative’ of the Palestinians, ending King Hussein’s claim. On 13 November 1974 Arafat addressed the UN General Assembly with the ‘gun and olive branch’ speech, and the PLO was granted permanent observer status.

The PLO Mini-State in Lebanon

After King Hussein expelled the PLO from Jordan in 1970–71, the leadership relocated to Lebanon, taking advantage of the 1969 Cairo Agreement that allowed armed Palestinian operations from Lebanese soil. By the mid-1970s the PLO ran what observers called ‘Fatahland’ in southern Lebanon — armed checkpoints, social services, courts, schools. In April 1975 a sectarian massacre on a Palestinian bus in Beirut helped touch off the Lebanese civil war. The Palestinians, mostly Sunni, fought alongside Lebanese leftist and Druze militias against the Maronite Christian Phalange. Syria intervened in 1976 with around 20,000 troops, switching sides as the conflict shifted. Lebanon ceased to function as a state, and the PLO acquired the freedom of action it had lost in Jordan.

Reprisals, the Litani Operation and UNIFIL

PLO rocket and cross-border raids drew Israeli reprisals throughout the 1970s. After a Fatah coastal raid killed thirty-eight Israelis on the Tel Aviv road in March 1978, Prime Minister Begin sent the IDF into southern Lebanon. The operation pushed PLO forces north of the Litani river and left a Christian-led Israeli proxy force, the ‘South Lebanon Army’, in control of a six-mile buffer zone. The UN Security Council passed Resolution 425 calling for Israeli withdrawal and authorised UNIFIL, the UN peacekeeping force still on the border today. The Israeli army withdrew — partially — but reprisals and rockets continued.

It is tempting to treat ‘the PLO’ and ‘the Palestinians’ as one block, but the spec rewards students who keep them distinct. The PLO was an umbrella body led by Arafat’s Fatah, but it also contained the Marxist-Leninist PFLP and other smaller factions, each with its own line. After Rabat 1974 the PLO was the diplomatic representative of the Palestinians, but it was an Arab-state-funded leadership living in Lebanon, not a government chosen by Palestinians on the West Bank or in Gaza. By 1987, when the Intifada broke out spontaneously among occupied Palestinians, the PLO leadership in Tunis was caught off guard. The collapse of the PLO’s Lebanese position in 1982, the topic of this lesson, set up that disconnect directly.

Operation Peace for Galilee, June 1982

On 3 June 1982 Palestinian gunmen of the Abu Nidal faction shot the Israeli ambassador to London, Shlomo Argov. Begin’s cabinet, with Defence Minister Ariel Sharon driving the planning, used the attack as the trigger for an invasion that had been prepared for months. Operation Peace for Galilee began on 6 June 1982. Sharon promised the cabinet a forty-kilometre advance to remove PLO artillery from northern Israel; in practice the IDF drove on to Beirut and besieged the western half of the city for ten weeks. An estimated 17,000 Lebanese and Palestinian civilians and combatants were killed during the 1982 invasion and siege. US envoy Philip Habib brokered an evacuation deal in August 1982: PLO fighters and headquarters staff would leave Lebanon under multinational supervision and disperse to eight Arab countries. About 14,000 PLO personnel left by ship; Arafat and his Fatah staff went to Tunis, more than 1,500 miles from any Palestinian territory.

Sabra and Shatila, September 1982

On 14 September 1982 the Christian Phalange leader and Lebanese President-elect Bashir Gemayel was assassinated. The IDF moved into West Beirut and let Phalange militias enter the Sabra and Shatila refugee camps to flush out remaining PLO fighters. Between the night of 16 September and the morning of 18 September the militiamen massacred between 700 and 3,500 unarmed Palestinian civilians. The IDF, which had ringed the camps with flares to light the area for the killers, did not intervene. The Israeli government’s own Kahan Commission reported in February 1983 that Israel bore ‘indirect responsibility’; Sharon was forced to resign as Defence Minister, though he remained in cabinet. About 400,000 Israelis — one in ten of the population — demonstrated against the war in Tel Aviv on 25 September 1982, the largest protest in Israel’s history.

Key Fact

Operation Peace for Galilee began on 6 June 1982. After a ten-week siege of Beirut the PLO leadership was evacuated to Tunis in August 1982. The Kahan Commission reported in February 1983 that Israel bore ‘indirect responsibility’ for the Sabra and Shatila massacre; Sharon resigned as Defence Minister.

Hezbollah and the New Map of Resistance

The 1982 invasion did not end Israel’s problem in Lebanon — it changed it. Iran sent Revolutionary Guards to the Bekaa Valley to organise Lebanon’s long-marginalised Shia community. The new movement, Hezbollah, used suicide truck bombs against the IDF, the multinational force and the US embassy. The October 1983 bombings of the US Marine and French paratrooper barracks killed 241 American and 58 French troops in a single morning. The multinational force withdrew. Israel pulled back to the south Lebanon ‘security zone’ in 1985 but stayed there until 2000. The PLO had been displaced as the symbol of armed resistance to Israel by a Shia movement Israel had not anticipated.

A common shorthand is that Israel won militarily in 1982 but lost politically. Examiner indicative content for the 2023 importance prompt rewards more granularity. The PLO had its mini-state, headquarters and roughly 14,000 fighters removed from a country bordering Israel. Arafat, in distant Tunis, was harder to reach but also harder to lead from. The vacuum was filled by Hezbollah and, on the West Bank itself by 1987, by Hamas, both of which rejected the PLO’s eventual two-state turn. Sabra and Shatila, the protests in Tel Aviv and the Kahan Commission marked the first sustained Israeli internal challenge to a war policy. The PLO was militarily defeated, diplomatically isolated in Tunis, and yet politically more central than ever — because no replacement representative existed. That contradiction set up the next two years.

The PLO Reset

From 1983 to 1987 the PLO leadership in Tunis tried to reach the Palestinians it could no longer touch directly. Arafat survived a Syrian-backed Fatah mutiny in 1983 and an Israeli air strike on his Tunis headquarters in October 1985. The Palestinian National Council in Algiers in 1987 began drafting language that would lead, in November 1988, to the formal renunciation of terrorism — the topic of the next lesson. By the time the Intifada began in December 1987, the PLO leadership was a distant authority that the children of Gaza throwing stones recognised only as a flag and a name. Lebanon had given the PLO a base; it had also stripped it down to the point where it would have to make compromises a stronger PLO would never have considered.

Strong answers analyse the loss of the PLO mini-state in southern Lebanon, the evacuation of around 14,000 fighters and the leadership to Tunis (1,500 miles from Palestinian territory), and the political space that opened for new groups (Hezbollah’s rise; Hamas’s founding in 1987). Always tie consequences back to the PLO specifically.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • At Rabat in October 1974 the Arab League made the PLO the ‘sole legitimate representative’ of the Palestinians; weeks later Arafat addressed the UN with the ‘gun and olive branch’ speech and the PLO was granted observer status.
  • From its Lebanese base the PLO drew Israeli reprisals: the 1978 Litani Operation produced UNIFIL and a buffer zone, and Operation Peace for Galilee in June 1982 reached Beirut, besieged the city for ten weeks and forced the PLO to evacuate to Tunis.
  • The Sabra and Shatila massacre of September 1982 produced the Kahan Commission’s ‘indirect responsibility’ finding and the largest protest in Israeli history; Hezbollah emerged from the Shia community of southern Lebanon, displacing the PLO as the leading armed challenge to Israel.

lessons.title: The First Intifada and Arafat's Turn, 1987–88
lessons.description: How a Gaza traffic accident became a four-year uprising and the PLO’s decisive political turn.
lessons.content_html:
Twenty Years of Occupation

By December 1987 the West Bank and Gaza Strip had been under Israeli military rule for twenty years. The Palestinian population had doubled. Around 60,000 Israeli settlers lived in roughly 130 settlements, and a network of bypass roads, military zones and water-allocation rules had hardened into what international lawyers called occupied territories. Permits regulated Palestinian work inside Israel; identity cards, military courts and curfews regulated almost everything else. The PLO leadership, exiled to Tunis since 1982, was 1,500 miles away. A new generation of Palestinians had grown up knowing only Israeli rule and a distant flag.

Key Fact

By 1987 the West Bank and Gaza had been under Israeli military rule for twenty years. The PLO leadership had been in Tunis since 1982. Around 60,000 Israeli settlers lived in roughly 130 West Bank settlements; the population now under occupation had roughly doubled since 1967.

Jabaliya, December 1987

On 8 December 1987 an Israeli army truck collided with two cars at the Erez crossing into Gaza, killing four Palestinian workers from Jabaliya refugee camp. Rumours spread that the crash was deliberate. The next day at the Jabaliya funerals turned into a riot; Israeli forces shot dead a seventeen-year-old. Within a week protests spread to every refugee camp in Gaza and to the West Bank. Schools closed; markets shuttered in commercial strikes. The Arabic press named what was happening the Intifada — literally ‘a shaking off’. It had not been planned by the PLO and it surprised them as much as it surprised the IDF.

Forms of Protest

The Intifada was driven from below by a network of local committees that came to be coordinated through the ‘Unified National Leadership of the Uprising’. Stone-throwing children became its public image, but the campaign also included general strikes, a boycott of Israeli goods, refusal to pay taxes (especially in the town of Beit Sahour), and the formation of unofficial Palestinian schools when Israeli authorities closed the official ones. Guns were deliberately kept off the streets in the early months; the strategy was civilian and visual. Defence Minister Yitzhak Rabin’s ‘iron fist’ response — mass arrests, school closures and an instruction in January 1988 to ‘break the bones’ of stone-throwers — produced television footage that turned international opinion against Israel for the first time on the scale it had hoped to avoid.

Students often write that ‘the PLO launched the Intifada’. The strongest answers, supported by examiner indicative content, recognise the opposite. The uprising emerged spontaneously from refugee camps in Gaza in December 1987, organised through local committees that had no contact with Tunis when it began. The Tunis leadership scrambled to keep up: Arafat’s December 1988 speech is best understood as the PLO catching up with developments inside the occupied territories rather than directing them. The same point matters for understanding Hamas, founded in Gaza in the same month the Intifada began — the PLO no longer had monopoly representation of the Palestinians in the territories.

Hamas, December 1987

In the same week that the Intifada broke out, Sheikh Ahmed Yassin and other leaders of the Gaza branch of the Muslim Brotherhood founded Hamas, the Islamic Resistance Movement. Hamas’s 1988 charter rejected any recognition of Israel and any negotiated settlement, positioning itself in direct opposition to a PLO that was already moving the other way. Hamas built its base through mosques and welfare networks (clinics, schools, food kitchens) that had operated semi-tolerated under Israel because they were seen as alternatives to the secular nationalist PLO. From 1987 onwards there was a Palestinian movement on the ground in Gaza that did not answer to Arafat and did not accept partition.

The Algiers Declaration of Independence, November 1988

In July 1988 King Hussein of Jordan formally renounced his claim to the West Bank, leaving the PLO with sole responsibility for negotiating its future. The Palestine National Council, the PLO’s parliament-in-exile, met in Algiers from 12 to 15 November 1988. On 15 November Arafat read the Algiers Declaration, proclaiming an independent Palestinian state. By citing UN Resolution 181 — the 1947 partition plan — as the legal basis, the PLO implicitly accepted, for the first time, the existence of an Israeli state alongside it. Within a month, around eighty states had recognised the new declaration of independence.

Geneva, December 1988

Arafat had been due to address the UN General Assembly in New York to make the next political move. The Reagan administration refused him a visa. The General Assembly voted to relocate the session to Geneva. On 13 December 1988 Arafat made the speech and the next day, on US insistence, made it again in plainer language. He recognised Israel’s right to exist within the 1967 borders; accepted UN Resolutions 242 and 338; and renounced terrorism in all its forms. Within hours the United States announced that it would open direct dialogue with the PLO. The legal block on US-PLO contact, in place since the 1970s, was gone.

Key Fact

On 13–14 December 1988, in Geneva, Arafat recognised Israel’s right to exist within the 1967 borders, accepted UN Resolutions 242 and 338 and renounced terrorism. The United States opened direct dialogue with the PLO within hours, ending nearly two decades of diplomatic isolation.

A Mixed Reception

The reception of Arafat’s turn was sharply split. Around the world, eighty-plus states had already recognised the Algiers declaration; the European Community welcomed the speech. The Israeli government of Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir refused to negotiate with the PLO, insisting Arafat’s words were tactical rather than strategic. Inside the territories Hamas rejected the renunciation entirely and began its own campaign of attacks. On the Israeli left a minority of politicians began to argue for talks with the PLO — the position that would, after Shamir’s 1992 election defeat, bring Yitzhak Rabin to the secret Oslo negotiations. The renunciation did not end the Intifada (which continued in declining intensity until 1993) and it did not produce immediate negotiations — but it removed the international diplomatic alibi for treating the PLO as untouchable.

The 2023 importance prompt asked specifically about Arafat’s renunciation for ‘attempts to find a solution in the Middle East’. Examiner mark schemes reward consequences for solution-seeking, not a description of the speech. Strong answers explain how the renunciation unlocked direct US-PLO dialogue (December 1988), normalised the idea of a two-state solution as the Palestinian position, and made the 1991 Madrid Conference and the 1993 Oslo Accords possible because the PLO could now be a recognised diplomatic partner. Weaker answers describe what Arafat said without showing what it caused.

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The First Intifada began with a Jabaliya traffic incident on 8 December 1987 and grew into a popular uprising of stone-throwing, strikes, tax revolts and civil disobedience that the PLO leadership in Tunis had not directed.
  • Hamas was founded in Gaza in December 1987 by Sheikh Ahmed Yassin and rejected any recognition of Israel, beginning a parallel Islamist track that would oppose every later peace process.
  • In November 1988 the PLO declared a Palestinian state on the basis of UN Resolution 181; in December 1988 in Geneva Arafat recognised Israel within 1967 borders, accepted UN 242 and renounced terrorism, and the United States opened direct PLO dialogue within hours.

lessons.title: Cold War End, the Gulf War and Oslo, 1989–95
lessons.description: From the Berlin Wall to the White House lawn: the unipolar moment that produced Oslo.
lessons.content_html:
The End of the Cold War

Between November 1989 and December 1991 the geopolitical map of the Middle East was rewritten by events thousands of miles away. The Berlin Wall came down; the Warsaw Pact dissolved; the Soviet Union itself ceased to exist on 26 December 1991. Arab states that had relied on Soviet weapons, advisers and political cover — Syria most of all, but also Iraq, Egypt before 1972 and South Yemen — lost their patron. The United States entered what one of its strategists called the unipolar moment. For the first time since 1945 there was no second great power to fund Arab rejectionism. Cold War alignments that had blocked every previous peace effort lost their force.

Key Fact

The Soviet Union dissolved on 26 December 1991. Syria and Iraq lost their main superpower patron; the United States entered a ‘unipolar moment’ with no Cold War rival to block diplomatic frameworks. Arab rejectionism lost the financial and political backing it had relied on for forty years.

Iraq, Kuwait and the PLO’s Mistake

On 2 August 1990 Iraq invaded and annexed Kuwait. President George H. W. Bush built a thirty-five-state coalition under UN Security Council Resolution 678 that included not only the NATO allies but Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Morocco — an Arab-state line-up that would have been impossible during the Cold War. Yasser Arafat, gambling on his domestic Palestinian audience, publicly supported Saddam Hussein. The Gulf states retaliated by expelling around 350,000 Palestinian guest workers from Kuwait alone after liberation; Saudi, Kuwaiti and Gulf Cooperation Council aid to the PLO was cut, leaving the organisation roughly $300 million a year poorer. Arafat’s 1990 alignment cost the PLO the Arab funding it had relied on since the late 1960s — a financial squeeze that pushed it towards negotiation by 1992.

The Gulf War, January–February 1991

The air campaign of the Gulf War began on 17 January 1991. Saddam attempted to break the Arab portion of the coalition by firing thirty-nine Scud missiles at Israeli cities — if Israel retaliated, Egypt, Syria and Saudi Arabia could not stand alongside the Israelis. Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, after intense US pressure and the deployment of US Patriot missiles in Tel Aviv, held back. The ground war began on 24 February and ended in a ceasefire one hundred hours later. The coalition held; the United States emerged as the only conceivable broker of any future Middle East settlement; and Israeli restraint had been visibly worth something to the United States, providing a debt the next administration could collect.

Students sometimes treat the Rabin-Arafat handshake as a sudden breakthrough. The strongest answers show the chain. The end of the Cold War removed Soviet support for Arab rejectionism. The Gulf War cost the PLO its Gulf state funding. The Madrid Conference of October 1991 brought every regional state to the same table for the first time. Rabin’s narrow election win in June 1992 put a Labour government willing to negotiate in office. Arafat, weakened in Tunis, was finally pliable. None of those four conditions had been present a decade earlier; together they made Oslo possible. Nothing about it was inevitable, but everything about it was caused.

Madrid, October 1991

From 30 October to 1 November 1991 the United States and the dying Soviet Union co-hosted the Madrid Conference. For the first time Israel, Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and a Palestinian delegation (formally part of the Jordanian delegation, with PLO members vetted by Israel) sat at the same negotiating table. Madrid produced no breakthrough but it set up bilateral tracks — Israeli-Syrian, Israeli-Lebanese, Israeli-Jordanian, Israeli-Palestinian — that ran in parallel for the next few years. The Madrid track was visible, multilateral, and slow; the deal that broke through came from a track no one in Madrid was watching.

The Norwegian Channel, 1992–93

In June 1992 Yitzhak Rabin’s Labour party won the Israeli election, narrowly displacing Shamir’s Likud. From January 1993 the Norwegian government hosted secret meetings outside Oslo between Israeli academics (later Israeli government negotiators) and PLO representatives. The two sides reached a draft Declaration of Principles in August 1993. On 9 September Arafat wrote to Rabin recognising Israel’s right to exist; Rabin replied recognising the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people. On 13 September 1993, on the South Lawn of the White House, Rabin and Arafat signed the Declaration of Principles in front of US President Bill Clinton, who hosted but did not negotiate. The reluctant handshake between Rabin and Arafat became the defining image of post-Cold War Middle East diplomacy.

Key Fact

The Oslo back-channel was hosted by Norway from January 1993. On 13 September 1993 Rabin and Arafat signed the Declaration of Principles in Washington with Clinton as host. The two sides exchanged letters of mutual recognition four days earlier; the agreement set out a five-year interim period and self-government for Gaza and Jericho first.

From Declaration to Authority

Implementation followed quickly. In May 1994 the Cairo Agreement transferred Gaza and Jericho to Palestinian self-government. The Palestinian National Authority took over civil administration; Arafat returned to Gaza on 1 July 1994 after twenty-seven years in exile. On 26 October 1994 King Hussein and Rabin signed the Israel-Jordan peace treaty, the second Arab-Israeli treaty after the 1979 Treaty of Washington. On 28 September 1995 Rabin and Arafat signed the Interim Agreement, known as Oslo II, in Washington. The agreement divided the West Bank into Areas A, B and C: A under full PA control, B under PA civil control and Israeli security, C under full Israeli control.

Rabin’s Assassination

Oslo had powerful Israeli opponents. Settler movements and right-wing rallies in 1994–95 portrayed Rabin as a traitor; some demonstrators waved posters of him in Nazi uniform. On 4 November 1995, after speaking at a peace rally in Tel Aviv’s Kings of Israel Square, Rabin was shot twice by Yigal Amir, a 25-year-old Jewish religious nationalist. He died on the operating table. Hamas, which had rejected the Oslo Accords from the start, escalated suicide bombings of Israeli buses and cafes in 1995–96. Shimon Peres lost the 1996 election by a fraction of a percent to Likud’s Benjamin Netanyahu, who had campaigned against the Accords. The Oslo process did not formally end in 1995; the political momentum behind it largely did.

Examiners reward students who separate two tracks at the spec’s 1995 endpoint. Bilateral peace between Israel and named Arab states held: the 1979 Egypt treaty was still in force, the 1994 Israel-Jordan treaty held, and Gulf states began informal contacts with Israel from the early 1990s. The Palestinian-Israeli track produced mutual recognition, a Palestinian Authority and the Areas A/B/C division of the West Bank — real institutional change — but the ‘final-status’ issues (refugees, Jerusalem, settlements, borders) were deferred indefinitely and never resolved. Strong answers say so plainly rather than judging the whole peace project a success or a failure.
lessons.exam_tip_html: An 8-mark Explain the Importance prompt on the Oslo Accords (1993) for the Palestinian issue rewards consequences-for-the-Palestinians, not a narrative. Strong answers explain the establishment of the Palestinian National Authority and Arafat’s return to Gaza in July 1994 as the first formal Palestinian self-government since 1948; the Areas A/B/C division of the West Bank as both a real transfer of authority and the basis of all subsequent disputes; and the deferred ‘final-status’ issues that meant Oslo did not deliver a Palestinian state. Pair an immediate consequence with a longer-term one.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The collapse of the Soviet Union in December 1991 ended Arab rejectionism’s superpower patron and produced the ‘unipolar moment’ in which the United States could broker frameworks without rival.
  • The 1991 Gulf War cost the PLO its Gulf state funding after Arafat backed Saddam, weakening it economically and politically; the Madrid Conference of October 1991 brought every regional state to the same negotiating table for the first time.
  • The Oslo Accords (Washington, 13 September 1993) produced mutual recognition between Israel and the PLO, the establishment of the Palestinian National Authority in 1994, the Israel-Jordan peace treaty in October 1994 and the Areas A/B/C division of the West Bank in Oslo II (1995); Rabin’s assassination in November 1995 stalled the political momentum that had produced them.

Write a narrative account analysing the road from the end of the Cold War to the Oslo Accords in the years 1989–93.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Gulf War (1991)
• the Madrid Conference (1991)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A coherent analytical narrative covering at least three aspects (e.g. the dissolution of the Soviet Union and the loss of Arab rejectionism’s patron; the Gulf War coalition and the PLO’s loss of Gulf funding; the Madrid Conference’s bilateral tracks; Rabin’s 1992 election win; the Norwegian back-channel and the September 1993 Declaration of Principles). Uses both stimulus points and adds independent material such as the mutual-recognition letters or the ‘unipolar moment’. Connects events through causation rather than sequencing. [7–8]
Secure: Three aspects addressed with clear analytical links; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer than three aspects (capped at this band per the cap rule). [3–4]
Emerging: A descriptive sequence with little or no analysis of how events connected. [1–2]

glossary_terms.definition: The period after the Soviet collapse, c.1991–2001, when the United States was the only superpower and could impose diplomatic frameworks without a rival to obstruct them.

The 1991 US-led coalition military operation that expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait following Saddam Hussein’s invasion of August 1990; it tested the post-Cold War security order and reshaped Middle Eastern alignments.

The October–November 1991 international peace conference in the Spanish capital, co-hosted by the US and the USSR; the first occasion on which Israel, Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and a Palestinian delegation sat at the same table.

The Israeli-PLO Declaration of Principles signed in Washington on 13 September 1993, providing for mutual recognition, a five-year interim period and Palestinian self-government in Gaza and Jericho first.
The Palestinian self-governing body established under the Oslo Accords from May 1994; assumed civil administration in parts of Gaza, Jericho and (after 1995) the major West Bank towns.
The peace treaty signed at Wadi Araba on 26 October 1994 between Israel and Jordan; ended the state of war and remains in force.
The three categories of West Bank territory created by Oslo II in 1995: A under full Palestinian Authority control; B under PA civil control and Israeli security; C under full Israeli control.
